summary: Return the minimum difference between the values of any two nodes of a BST.
mainInsight: An in-order traversal of a BST yields values in sorted order, and in a sorted list the minimum gap is always between neighbours. So track the previous in-order value and take min(cur - prev).
invariant: When a node is visited in order, prev holds the largest value smaller than it seen so far (its in-order predecessor).

approaches.summary: Any traversal, then check every pair.

approaches.name: Collect and sort
weaknesses: Sorting is wasted on a BST
approaches.interviewRelevance: Fine but misses the BST property.

approaches.name: In-order traversal with previous value
approaches.summary: In-order visit; compare each node with the previous visited value.

commonMistakes: Comparing each node only with its direct children (the closest value may be far away in the tree).
Forgetting the prev is None check on the first visited node.
Using pre-order or post-order, which do not give sorted order.
edgeCases: Closest pair is a node and its in-order predecessor deep in the left subtree's right spine.

promptVariants: Why is comparing each node with its two children not enough?
What is wrong with taking min(|node - child|) over all parent-child pairs?
options: The closest pair may not be parent and child
Children can have equal values in a BST
It misses the root's value entirely
It is correct but slower than in-order
cards.answer: The closest pair may not be parent and child
cards.explanation: The root's in-order neighbour is the rightmost node of its left subtree, which can be several levels below it.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Children can have equal values in a BST: Values are distinct here and that is not the failure.
incorrectOptionExplanations.It misses the root's value entirely: The root is compared with its children; the issue is non-adjacent pairs.
incorrectOptionExplanations.It is correct but slower than in-order: It is the same speed but gives wrong answers.

promptVariants: root = [90, 69, null, 49, 89, null, 52]. What is returned?
For the BST [90, 69, null, 49, 89, null, 52], what is the minimum difference?
cards.explanation: In-order: 49, 52, 69, 89, 90. Gaps are 3, 17, 20, 1, so the answer is 1, between the root 90 and 89, its in-order predecessor two levels down (89 is a child of 69, not of 90).

incorrectOptionExplanations.3: 49 and 52 differ by 3, but 89 and 90 are closer.
incorrectOptionExplanations.20: That is 89 - 69, a parent-child gap, not the minimum.
incorrectOptionExplanations.21: That is 90 - 69, the root and its child.

promptVariants: Which property of a BST makes the one-pass solution possible?
Why does tracking only the previous value suffice?
options: In-order traversal visits values in sorted order
Every left child is exactly one less than its parent
The root holds the median of all values
Leaves always hold the smallest differences
cards.answer: In-order traversal visits values in sorted order
cards.explanation: Sorted order means the minimum gap is between consecutive values, and the previous in-order value is the consecutive one.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Every left child is exactly one less tha: Only less than, not by exactly one.
incorrectOptionExplanations.The root holds the median of all values: A BST need not be balanced.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Leaves always hold the smallest differen: The closest pair can involve internal nodes.

promptVariants: What is the time complexity of the canonical code?
Derive the running time of the in-order solution.
cards.explanation: Each node is visited once with O(1) work.

incorrectOptionExplanations.O(h): That is the stack space, not the time.

promptVariants: The recursion stack uses O(___) space, the tree height.
Extra space of the recursive in-order: O(___).
cards.explanation: Depth equals the height: log n if balanced, n for a skewed tree. Morris traversal would make it O(1).
